claim: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) is an obligatory gate for the production of vocalizations in all mammals.
source: Work from the last five decades has established the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) as an obligatory gate for the production of vocalizations in all mammals (Fenzl and Schuller, 2002; Jürgens, 1994; Jürgens, 2002; Jürgens, 2009; Subramanian, et al., 2020; Sugiyama et al., 2010; Tschida et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this finding over five decades

claim: Forebrain inputs to the PAG regulate the production of vocalizations in a context-dependent fashion.
source: it is thought that forebrain inputs to the PAG regulate the production of vocalizations in a context-dependent fashion
evidence: Stated as a theoretical framework based on established understanding

claim: Forebrain regions including the cortex, amygdala, and hypothalamus have been implicated in regulating vocalization as a function of social context.
source: In line with this idea, forebrain regions including the cortex, amygdala, and hypothalamus have been implicated in regulating vocalization as a function of social context (Bennett et al., 2019; Dujardin and Jürgens, 2006; Gao et al., 2019; Green et al., 2018; Jürgens, 1982; Jürgens, 2002; Kyuhou and Gemba, 1998; Ma and Kanwal, 2014; Manteuffel et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Electrical or pharmacological activation of various forebrain regions can elicit vocalizations.
source: Notably, although electrical or pharmacological activation of various forebrain regions can elicit vocalizations (Jürgens, 2009; Jürgens and Ploog, 1970; Jürgens and Richter, 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: The effects of forebrain activation on vocalization depend on an intact PAG.
source: these effects depend on an intact PAG (Jürgens and Pratt, 1979; Lu and Jürgens, 1993; Siebert and Jürgens, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: The PAG acts as an essential hub for descending forebrain control of vocalization.
source: suggesting that the PAG acts as an essential hub for descending forebrain control of vocalization
evidence: Inferred from cited studies showing dependence on intact PAG

claim: The synaptic mechanisms through which forebrain neurons interact with the PAG vocal gating circuit to either promote or suppress vocalization remain unknown.
source: Despite the centrality of the PAG to vocalization, the synaptic mechanisms through which forebrain neurons interact with the PAG vocal gating circuit to either promote or suppress vocalization remain unknown
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: The PAG is a functionally heterogeneous structure important to many survival behaviors.
source: The PAG is a functionally heterogeneous structure important to many survival behaviors (Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Carrive, 1993; Evans et al., 2018; Holstege, 2014; Tovote et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: PAG-USV neurons were identified using an intersectional activity-dependent genetic tagging technique.
source: we recently used an intersectional activity-dependent genetic tagging technique to identify neurons in the PAG of the mouse that gate the production of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs; i.e. PAG-USV neurons Tschida et al., 2019)
evidence: Refers to a prior study by the authors using a specific experimental method

claim: Mice produce ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in a variety of social contexts.
source: which mice produce in a variety of social contexts (Chabout et al., 2015; Holy and Guo, 2005; Maggio and Whitney, 1985; Neunuebel et al., 2015; Nyby, 1979; Portfors and Perkel, 2014; Whitney et al., 1974)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Transsynaptic tracing from PAG-USV neurons was performed only in male mice due to the difficulty in eliciting robust and reliable USVs from female mice.
source: Due to the difficulty in eliciting robust and reliable USVs from female mice, transsynaptic tracing from CANE-tagged PAG-USV neurons was performed only in male mice
evidence: Explanation of experimental design choice based on practical considerations

claim: Transsynaptic tracing revealed monosynaptic inputs to PAG-USV neurons from a variety of forebrain areas.
source: These rabies tracing experiments revealed monosynaptic inputs to PAG-USV neurons as well as to local GABAergic PAG neurons from a variety of forebrain areas (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from rabies tracing experiments and referenced figures

claim: The hypothalamus and amygdala are important for the regulation and production of emotional and social behaviors, including vocalization.
source: We subsequently focused on thoroughly characterizing forebrain afferents from the hypothalamus and amygdala, two brain regions important for the regulation and production of emotional and social behaviors, including vocalization (Chen and Hong, 2018; Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Ehrlich et al., 2009; Gothard, 2020; Janak and Tye, 2015; LeDoux, 2007; Sternson, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The majority (~84%) of PAG-projecting POA neurons are GABAergic.
source: This experiment revealed that the majority (~84%, Figure 1C–D) of PAG-projecting POA neurons (i.e. POAPAG neurons) and almost all (~98%, Figure 1D) of PAG-projecting AmgC/M and CeA neurons (i.e. AmgC/M-PAG and CeAPAG neurons) are GABAergic
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: Almost all (~98%) of PAG-projecting AmgC/M and CeA neurons are GABAergic.
source: This experiment revealed that the majority (~84%, Figure 1C–D) of PAG-projecting POA neurons (i.e. POAPAG neurons) and almost all (~98%, Figure 1D) of PAG-projecting AmgC/M and CeA neurons (i.e. AmgC/M-PAG and CeAPAG neurons) are GABAergic
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The PAG vocal gating circuit receives input from inhibitory neurons in both the preoptic hypothalamus and the amygdala.
source: In summary, the PAG vocal gating circuit receives input from inhibitory neurons in both the preoptic hypothalamus and the amygdala
evidence: Summary statement based on the neurotransmitter phenotype data presented

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG cell bodies was sufficient to elicit USVs in male and female mice that were singly tested in the absence of social partners or social cues.
source: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG cell bodies was sufficient to elicit USVs in male and female mice that were singly tested in the absence of social partners or social cues (USVs elicited in N = 6 of 8 males, N = 3 of 4 females; 10 Hz trains or tonic pulses of 1–2 s duration; Figure 2A–B, Video 1)
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and Video 1

claim: The efficacy of optogenetic stimulation of POAPAG neurons and the latency from stimulation to USV onset were variable both within and across individual mice.
source: Although optogenetic activation of POAPAG neurons often elicited robust USV production, the efficacy of optogenetic stimulation (number of USVs elicited per trial, number of successful trials) as well as the latency from stimulation to USV onset were variable both within and across individual mice (Figure 2B and F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in referenced figures

claim: Delivery of blue light to the POA of GFP-expressing mice failed to elicit USVs.
source: This vocal effect was specifically attributable to optogenetic activation of the POA, as delivery of blue light to the POA of GFP-expressing mice failed to elicit USVs (AAV-FLEX-GFP injected into the POA of Esr1-Cre males, see below for additional Esr1-Cre data, N = 5, Figure 2F)
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG neurons is capable of promoting USV production in both male and female mice.
source: In summary, optogenetic activation of POAPAG neurons is capable of promoting USV production in both male and female mice, consistent with the known role of the POA in promoting appetitive courtship behaviors
evidence: Summary of experimental findings with reference to established knowledge about POA function

claim: The majority of POAPAG neurons co-express Estrogen Receptor 1 (Esr1).
source: We also noted that the majority of POAPAG neurons co-express Estrogen Receptor 1 (Esr1), a prominent marker for neurons in the POA (278/319 Figure 2C; Fang et al., 2018; Moffitt et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior research

claim: Optogenetically activating Esr1+ POA neurons was sufficient to elicit USV production in male and female mice tested in the absence of any social partners or social cues.
source: We observed that optogenetically activating Esr1+ POA neurons was sufficient to elicit USV production in male (N = 4 of 5) and female mice (N = 3 of 4) that were tested in the absence of any social partners or social cues (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Optogenetic activation of VGlut2+ neurons within the POA failed to elicit USV production.
source: In contrast, optogenetic activation of VGlut2+ neurons within the POA failed to elicit USV production (Figure 2F, N = 3 males, POA of VGlut-Cre mice injected with AAV-FLEX-ChR2)
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Optogenetic activation of GABAergic POA neurons elicits USV production in male and female mice.
source: Our findings confirm and extend the recent finding that optogenetic activation of GABAergic POA neurons elicits USV production in male and female mice (Gao et al., 2019)
evidence: Confirmation of findings from a cited prior study

claim: Bilateral Esr1+ POAPAG terminal activation within the PAG was sufficient to elicit USV production.
source: Bilateral Esr1+ POAPAG terminal activation within the PAG was sufficient to elicit USV production (N = 1 of 2 males; N = 4 of 6 females, 20 Hz trains of 2–10 s duration)
evidence: Supported by optogenetic terminal activation experimental data

claim: Optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA axon terminals within the PAG evoked escape behavior in four of eight tested animals.
source: This treatment also evoked escape behavior in four of eight of the tested animals, which was not observed following optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA cell bodies, suggesting that viral spread to PAG-projecting neurons nearby to the POA may account for these effects
evidence: Experimental observation with inference about potential confound

claim: USVs were not elicited by optogenetically activating Esr1+ POA axon terminals in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: In fact, USVs were not elicited by optogenetically activating either Esr1+ POA axon terminals in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Figure 2F, 0/2 females, 0/2 males)
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 2F

claim: USVs were not elicited by optogenetically activating PAG-projecting neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH).
source: or PAG-projecting neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) (Figure 2F, 0/3 males, AAV-retro-Cre injected in the PAG, AAV-FLEX-ChR2 injected in the VMH)
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 2F

claim: GABAergic POA neurons, including Esr1+ cells, act via their synapses in the caudolateral PAG to promote USV production.
source: Therefore, GABAergic POA neurons, including Esr1+ cells, act via their synapses in the caudolateral PAG to promote USV production
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing specificity of effects

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG neurons drove a slightly negative place preference on average.
source: We observed that optogenetic activation of POAPAG neurons drove a slightly negative place preference on average (mean PP = 0.39 +/- 0.07 for N = 7 mice; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, panel A)
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA cell bodies did not positively reinforce place preference.
source: and that optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA cell bodies did not positively reinforce place preference (mean PP = 0.46 +/- 0.02 for N = 5 mice)
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data

claim: Optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA axon terminals within the VTA positively reinforced place preference.
source: In contrast, optogenetic activation of Esr1+ POA axon terminals within the VTA positively reinforced place preference (mean PP = 0.59 +/- 0.06, N = 4 mice, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, panel A)
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Optogenetic activation of either POAPAG or Esr1+ POA neurons did not drive mounting of other mice.
source: We also note that when using the same stimulation parameters that were sufficient to elicit USVs, optogenetic activation of either POAPAG or Esr1+ POA neurons did not drive mounting of other mice (N = 7 POAPAG-ChR2 mice tested; N = 4 POA-Esr1-ChR2 mice tested)
evidence: Behavioral observation from optogenetic experiments

claim: Optogenetic activation of either POAPAG or Esr1+ POA neurons did not induce overt locomotion.
source: nor did it induce overt locomotion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, panel B)
evidence: Behavioral observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Activation of POAPAG neurons can elicit USVs in a manner that does not depend on positive reinforcement and without recruiting other courtship behaviors.
source: These experiments indicate that activation of POAPAG neurons can elicit USVs in a manner that does not depend on positive reinforcement and without recruiting other courtship behaviors
evidence: Conclusion drawn from place preference and behavioral data

claim: The minimum and mean latencies to elicit USVs by optogenetic stimulation of POA neurons were 664.5 +/- 320.9 ms and 1782.6 +/- 407.6 ms, respectively.
source: Indeed, we found that the minimum and mean latencies to elicit USVs by optogenetic stimulation of POA neurons were 664.5 +/- 320.9 ms and 1782.6 +/- 407.6 ms, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, calculated from N = 9 POAPAG-ChR2 and N = 7 POA-Esr1-ChR2 mice)
evidence: Quantitative data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The latencies to elicit USVs by optogenetic stimulation of POA neurons are longer than those observed when optogenetically activating PAG-USV neurons.
source: These latencies are longer than those observed when optogenetically activating PAG-USV neurons (PAG-USV activation: min. latency from laser onset to first USV was 23.4 ± 8.6 ms, mean latency was 406.6 ± 0.5 ms) (Tschida et al., 2019)
evidence: Comparison of current data to data from a cited prior study

claim: The latencies from optogenetic activation of the hypothalamus to observed effects on behavior are comparable to those reported in other studies.
source: but are comparable to the latencies from optogenetic activation of the hypothalamus to observed effects on behavior that have been reported in other studies (Lin et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2018)
evidence: Comparison to data from cited prior studies

claim: USV bouts elicited by optogenetic activation of the POA often outlasted the duration of the optogenetic stimulation, sometimes by many seconds.
source: We also found that USV bouts elicited by optogenetic activation of the POA often outlasted the duration of the optogenetic stimulation, sometimes by many seconds (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in referenced figures

claim: USV bout durations following optogenetic activation of PAG-USV neurons map on tightly to the duration of optogenetic stimulation.
source: This contrasts with what is observed following optogenetic activation of PAG-USV neurons, in which USV bout durations map on tightly to the duration of optogenetic stimulation (Tschida et al., 2019)
evidence: Comparison to data from a cited prior study

claim: Brief optogenetic stimulation in the POA can be transformed into longer lasting changes in neural activity within the POA or across POA-to-PAG synapses.
source: and suggests that brief optogenetic stimulation in the POA can be transformed into longer lasting changes in neural activity within the POA or across POA-to-PAG synapses
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation about USV bout durations

claim: The VAE converged on a concise latent representation of only five dimensions for USV spectrograms.
source: We applied this approach to spectrograms of USVs to compare the acoustic features of female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs from the same mice and found that the VAE converged on a concise latent representation of only five dimensions
evidence: Result from computational analysis using VAE method

claim: For some mice, female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs were acoustically similar.
source: This analysis revealed that for some mice, female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs were acoustically similar (Figure 3C, left)
evidence: Result from VAE analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: For some mice, a subset of optogenetically elicited USVs were acoustically distinct from female-directed USVs.
source: while for other mice, a subset of optogenetically elicited USVs were acoustically distinct from female-directed USVs (Figure 3C, right)
evidence: Result from VAE analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: There are significantly larger differences between female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs than expected by variability within the female-directed recording sessions alone.
source: A paired comparison revealed significantly larger differences between female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs than expected by variability within the female-directed recording sessions alone (Figure 3D, two-sided, continuity-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W = 5, p<0.01)
evidence: Statistical analysis of MMD data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The differences between female-directed and optogenetically elicited USVs are larger than expected by across-day variability in female-directed recording sessions from control animals.
source: or than expected by across-day variability in female-directed recording sessions from control animals (gray points, Figure 3D, female-directed USVs were recorded on 2 different days from N = 10 control mice, p=0.003 for difference between female-directed vs. female-directed in control mice and opto vs. female-directed in experimental mice, Mann Whitney U test)
evidence: Statistical comparison to control data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Many USVs elicited by optogenetic activation of POA neurons resemble female-directed USVs, although a subset differs in their acoustic features.
source: In conclusion, many USVs elicited by optogenetic activation of POA neurons resemble female-directed USVs, although a subset differs in their acoustic features from USVs found in the animals' female-directed repertoires
evidence: Summary conclusion from acoustic analysis data

claim: Optogenetically-elicited USVs and female-directed USVs are largely acoustically overlapping except in one region of the UMAP representation.
source: When the latent representations of these two types of USVs were plotted together for all mice in our dataset, it became clear that optogenetically-elicited USVs and female-directed USVs are largely acoustically overlapping except in one region of the UMAP representation (upper middle portion of Figure 3E, dominated by blue points)
evidence: Observation from UMAP visualization shown in Figure 3E

claim: Only 20% of condition information (optogenetically elicited versus female-directed) can be predicted by latent syllable descriptions.
source: Despite this outlying region of acoustically distinct optogenetically elicited USVs, we conservatively estimate that only 20% of condition information (optogenetically elicited versus female-directed) can be predicted by latent syllable descriptions, consistent with largely overlapping distributions of natural and optogenetically elicited USVs (0.20 bits, fivefold class-balanced logistic regression)
evidence: Result from machine learning classification analysis

claim: The acoustically unusual optogenetically elicited USVs tended to be louder and had greater frequency bandwidths than female-directed USVs.
source: This analysis revealed that the acoustically unusual optogenetically elicited USVs tended to be louder and had greater frequency bandwidths than female-directed USVs
evidence: Result from analysis of acoustic features shown in Figure 3F

claim: Optogenetically-elicited USVs differed from female-directed USVs in a manner that was consistent across mice.
source: A shuffle test revealed significantly larger alignment between these vectors than expected by chance (mean cosine similarity = 0.50, p<1e-5), indicating that optogenetically-elicited USVs differed from female-directed USVs in a manner that was consistent across mice
evidence: Statistical analysis showing consistency across animals

claim: Optogenetic activation of the POA elicits USVs whose acoustic features are largely overlapping with those of female-directed USVs produced by the same animal.
source: In summary, optogenetic activation of the POA elicits USVs whose acoustic features are largely overlapping with those of female-directed USVs produced by the same animal, despite the artificiality inherent to optogenetic stimulation
evidence: Summary conclusion from acoustic analysis

claim: The viral strategy designed to express ChR2 in PAG-projecting AmgC/M and CeA neurons failed to label neurons in the CeA and instead only labeled AmgC/M neurons.
source: Surprisingly, given the strong transsynaptic labeling of both the CeA and AmgC/M achieved with modified rabies tracing from the PAG vocal gating circuit, we found that this viral strategy failed to label neurons in the CeA and instead only labeled AmgC/M neurons, whose cell bodies reside medial to the CeA and dorsal to the medial amygdala (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Observation from viral labeling experiments shown in referenced figures

claim: The restricted labeling pattern was due to restricted tropism of the AAV-retro-Cre virus and not to inaccurate targeting of the CeA.
source: To ensure that this labeling pattern was due to restricted tropism of the AAV-retro-Cre virus and not to inaccurate targeting of the CeA, we repeated the injections of the AAV-retro-Cre virus in the PAG of a Cre-dependent tdTomato reporter mouse. Again, we observed cell body labeling in the AmgC/M but not in the CeA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The AAV-retro-Cre virus can infect AmgC/M but not CeA neurons.
source: suggesting that in contrast to the modified rabies virus used in the transsynaptic tracing from the PAG vocal gating circuit, the AAV-retro-Cre virus can infect AmgC/M but not CeA neurons
evidence: Inference from comparison of labeling patterns with different viral vectors

claim: Optogenetic activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons failed to elicit USV production in isolated mice.
source: Optogenetic activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons failed to elicit USV production and also did not drive any other obvious behavioral effects (Videos 2, 3, 4)
evidence: Behavioral observation from optogenetic experiments shown in Videos 2, 3, 4

claim: When AmgC/M-PAG neurons were optogenetically activated in male mice that were actively courting females and vocalizing, USV production was immediately and reversibly suppressed.
source: However, when AmgC/M-PAG neurons were optogenetically activated in male mice that were actively courting females and vocalizing, USV production was immediately and reversibly suppressed (Figure 4B, N = 8 mice)
evidence: Experimental data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: The suppressive effect of AmgC/M-PAG neuron activation on USV production was restricted to the period when these neurons were being optogenetically stimulated.
source: This suppressive effect was restricted to the period when AmgC/M-PAG neurons were being optogenetically stimulated, and USV production rebounded following the end of the optogenetic stimulation period (Figure 4B)
evidence: Temporal analysis of USV suppression shown in Figure 4B

claim: Most AmgC/M-PAG neurons are GABAergic (~92% express VGAT).
source: After using in situ hybridization to confirm that most AmgC/M-PAG neurons are GABAergic (~92% AmgC/M-PAG neurons express VGAT, Figure 4C)
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Optogenetic activation of GABAergic AmgC/M-PAG neurons robustly suppressed the male's USV production during courtship encounters with a female.
source: we used a similar intersectional viral strategy to express ChR2 selectively in GABAergic AmgC/M-PAG neurons (Figure 4D, AAV-retro-FLEX-ChR2 injected into the PAG of a VGAT-Cre mouse). With this strategy, we found that optogenetic activation of GABAergic AmgC/M-PAG neurons robustly suppressed the male's USV production during courtship encounters with a female (Figure 4D, N = 4 male mice)
evidence: Experimental data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4D

claim: Bilateral terminal activation of GABAergic AmgC/M-PAG neurons within the PAG was sufficient to suppress USV production.
source: Finally, we tested the effects on vocal behavior of optogenetically activating the axon terminals of GABAergic AmgC/M-PAG neurons within the PAG (Figure 4D). Such bilateral terminal activation was also sufficient to suppress USV production (in N = 3 of 3 males; Figure 4D)
evidence: Experimental data from optogenetic terminal activation shown in Figure 4D

claim: Mice exhibited neither freezing nor fleeing during optogenetic stimulation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons.
source: Mice exhibited neither freezing nor fleeing during optogenetic stimulation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons and, more notably, they usually continued to follow and sniff the female during the laser stimulation periods (Video 5; distance between male and female did not increase during optogenetic stimulation, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, panel B)
evidence: Behavioral observation from optogenetic experiments shown in Video 5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The change in USV production rates driven by optogenetic activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons was different from the change in spontaneous USV rates over time in control mice.
source: We also confirmed that the change in USV production rates driven by the optogenetic activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons was different from the change in spontaneous USV rates over time in mice that did not receive laser stimulation (Figure 4D, black trace), the change in USV rates over time in GFP control mice (Figure 4D, green trace), and the change in USV rates over time in AmgC/M-PAG-ChR2-expressing mice that were connected to a dummy ferrule that only shined blue light over their head (Figure 4D, gray trace; p<0.01 for differences between ChR2 groups vs. control groups during laser time, p>0.05 for differences between groups in post-laser period; two-way ANOVA with repeated measures on one factor, p<0.01 for interaction between group and time, followed by post-hoc pairwise Tukey's HSD tests)
evidence: Statistical comparison to multiple control conditions shown in Figure 4D

claim: Activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons does not drive a negative place preference.
source: Finally, we performed real-time place preference tests in which AmgC/M-PAG neurons were optogenetically activated when mice were in one of two sides of a test chamber (AmgC/M-PAG neurons were labeled with either the AAV-retro-Cre or the AAV-retro-ChR2 viral strategies). This experiment revealed that activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons does not drive a negative place preference (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, panel A)
evidence: Real-time place preference test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Activating AmgC/M-PAG neurons transiently and selectively suppresses USVs produced by male mice during courtship, an effect that cannot be accounted for by the mouse being put into a fearful or aversive state.
source: In summary, activating AmgC/M-PAG neurons transiently and selectively suppresses USVs produced by male mice during courtship, an effect that cannot be accounted for by the mouse being put into a fearful or aversive state
evidence: Summary conclusion from behavioral and place preference data

claim: POAPAG and AmgC/M-PAG neurons provide dense projections to a variety of dopaminergic cell groups, including the VTA, SNc and retrorubral/A8 region.
source: We observed dense projections from both POAPAG and AmgC/M-PAG neurons to a variety of dopaminergic cell groups, including the VTA, SNc and retrorubral/A8 region
evidence: Anatomical observation from axonal tracing experiments

claim: AmgC/M-PAG neurons provide input to the lateral preoptic area.
source: We also note that AmgC/M-PAG neurons provide input to the lateral preoptic area (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, top left)
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: POAPAG neurons provide input to the same region in which AmgC/M-PAG cell bodies reside.
source: while POAPAG neurons provide input to the same region in which AmgC/M-PAG cell bodies reside (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, middle left)
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: POAPAG and AmgC/M-PAG neurons have dense and overlapping terminal fields within the caudolateral PAG.
source: As expected, we also observed dense and overlapping terminal fields from both of the cell groups within the caudolateral PAG (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, bottom right)
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Activating AmgC/M-PAG axons evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in a majority (16/29) of mCherry-labeled PAG-USV neurons.
source: Activating AmgC/M-PAG terminals evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in a majority (16/29) of the mCherry-labeled PAG-USV neurons from which we recorded (mean current = 180.3 pA at 0 mV in TTX/4AP)
evidence: Electrophysiological recording data from brain slice experiments

claim: The evoked IPSCs from AmgC/M-PAG terminals onto PAG-USV neurons were completely abolished by application of the GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine.
source: These evoked IPSCs were completely abolished by application of the GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine (Figure 5E–F)
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 5E-F

claim: No optogenetically elicited EPSCs were detected when recording at −70 mV, the chloride reversal potential.
source: No optogenetically elicited EPSCs were detected when recording at −70 mV, the chloride reversal potential
evidence: Electrophysiological recording observation

claim: AmgC/M-PAG activity suppresses ongoing USV production by directly inhibiting PAG-USV neurons.
source: These findings support the idea that AmgC/M-PAG activity suppresses ongoing USV production by directly inhibiting PAG-USV neurons
evidence: Conclusion drawn from electrophysiological data

claim: Optical stimulation of POAPAG axons with blue-light-evoked IPSCs in the majority (26/36) of voltage clamped GABAergic PAG neurons.
source: Optical stimulation of POAPAG axons with blue-light-evoked IPSCs in the majority (26/36) of voltage clamped GABAergic PAG neurons from which we recorded (mean current = 328.8 pA at 0 mV) (Figure 6C)
evidence: Electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The evoked IPSCs from POAPAG axons onto GABAergic PAG neurons persisted upon application of TTX/4AP and were blocked by gabazine.
source: These evoked IPSCs persisted upon application of TTX/4AP and were blocked by gabazine, indicating that POAPAG axons make inhibitory synapses directly onto GABAergic PAG neurons (Figure 6D)
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 6D

claim: POAPAG axons make inhibitory synapses directly onto GABAergic PAG neurons.
source: indicating that POAPAG axons make inhibitory synapses directly onto GABAergic PAG neurons (Figure 6D)
evidence: Conclusion from electrophysiological and pharmacological data

claim: Optogenetically activating local VGAT+ neurons evoked IPSCs in almost all (13/16) of the PAG-USV neurons recorded.
source: Optogenetically activating local VGAT+ neurons evoked IPSCs in almost all (13/16) of the PAG-USV neurons from which we recorded (mean current = 579.9 pA at 0 mV in TTX/4AP) and these currents were completely abolished by application of gabazine (Figure 6G–H)
evidence: Electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 6G-H

claim: There is a functional connection between local inhibitory neurons and the PAG-USV neurons that gate USV production.
source: This experiment confirms the presence of a functional connection between local inhibitory neurons and the PAG-USV neurons that gate USV production
evidence: Conclusion from electrophysiological data

claim: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG terminals evoked IPSCs in only 1 of 23 PAG-USV neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of POAPAG terminals evoked IPSCs in only 1 of 23 PAG-USV neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, panel B)
evidence: Electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: POAPAG neurons appear to provide fewer or weaker synaptic inputs to PAG-USV neurons than to nearby GABAergic PAG neurons.
source: Although there are caveats to interpreting a low probability of synaptic connection in brain slices, POAPAG neurons appear to provide fewer or weaker synaptic inputs to PAG-USV neurons than to nearby GABAergic PAG neurons
evidence: Inference from comparison of connection probabilities with caveats noted

claim: POAPAG neurons primarily act through PAG interneurons to disinhibit PAG-USV neurons and promote USV production.

claim: Sex differences in the density, synaptic organization, and gene expression patterns of POA neurons might contribute to sexually dimorphic vocal behavior.
source: Although it remains unknown which factors might drive differential activation of male and female POAPAG neurons, it is possible that sex differences in the density (Campi et al., 2013; Gorski et al., 1978; Orikasa and Sakuma, 2010; Panzica et al., 1996), synaptic organization (Raisman and Field, 1971), and gene expression patterns (Moffitt et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2012), including those of sex hormone receptors (Cao and Patisaul, 2011) of POA neurons, might all contribute to this sexually dimorphic behavior (for a review, see Lenz et al., 2012)
evidence: Speculation based on cited prior research on sex differences in POA

claim: Male and female brains contain latent circuits for sex-typical behaviors that can be unmasked by artificial neural activation but that are gated in a sex-specific manner during natural behavior.
source: More broadly, our findings add to a growing body of literature indicating that male and female brains contain latent circuits for sex-typical behaviors that can be unmasked by artificial neural activation but that are gated in a sex-specific manner during natural behavior (Clyne and Miesenböck, 2008; Gao et al., 2019; Rezával et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018)
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of cited prior research

claim: The use of lower intensity optical stimulation may account for the difference in mounting behavior compared to a previous study.

claim: The majority of optogenetically elicited vocalizations fall within the distribution of naturally produced USVs.

claim: PAG-USV neurons gate USV production but do not directly pattern the acoustic content of vocalizations.
source: This finding provides further experimental support for a model in which the PAG-USV neurons that are disinhibited by input from the POA gate USV production but do not directly pattern the acoustic content of vocalizations

claim: Synchronous optogenetic activation of POA neurons may activate the PAG vocal gating circuit more strongly than occurs during natural behavior.
source: We found that these unusual optogenetically elicited USVs were louder and greater in frequency bandwidth, which we speculate may arise because synchronous optogenetic activation of POA neurons activates the PAG vocal gating circuit more strongly than occurs during natural behavior
evidence: Speculation based on acoustic analysis findings

claim: The USVs elicited by optogenetic stimulation of POAPAG neurons may be more similar acoustically to spontaneous USVs emitted in response to stationary social cues rather than to a mobile female partner.
source: Another possibility is that because the mice in our experiments were singly tested in the absence of social partners and thus typically were not moving at high speeds during optogenetic stimulation, the USVs elicited by optogenetic stimulation of POAPAG neurons may be more similar acoustically to spontaneous USVs emitted in response to stationary social cues, such as female urine, rather than in response to a mobile female partner
evidence: Speculation based on experimental conditions and prior research

claim: USVs produced by males in response to female urine were louder and had greater frequency bandwidth than those produced to female social partners.
source: Interestingly, a previous study found that the USVs produced by males in response to female urine were louder and had greater frequency bandwidth than those produced to female social partners (Chabout et al., 2015)

claim: AmgC/M-PAG neurons make inhibitory synapses on PAG-USV neurons.
source: We found that AmgC/M-PAG neurons make inhibitory synapses on PAG-USV neurons, which in turn gate vocalizations by exciting downstream vocal-respiratory pattern generating circuits (Tschida et al., 2019)
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological findings with reference to prior work

claim: The AmgC/M to PAG pathway provides a monosynaptic substrate through which vocalizations can be rapidly and effectively suppressed.
source: Thus, the AmgC/M to PAG pathway provides a monosynaptic substrate through which vocalizations can be rapidly and effectively suppressed

claim: Descending inhibitory inputs onto PAG-USV neurons may act rapidly to suppress vocalization in behavioral contexts in which vocalizing is risky or otherwise adverse.

claim: AmgC/M projections to other PAG cell types may modulate diverse behaviors in addition to vocalization.
source: We also note that while optogenetic activation of AmgC/M-PAG neurons transiently suppressed vocalization without obvious effects on non-vocal social behaviors and movement, it is possible that AmgC/M projections to other PAG cell types modulate diverse behaviors in addition to vocalization

claim: Disinhibition of glutamatergic projection neurons is a prominent circuit motif within the PAG for releasing a variety of behaviors.
source: Indeed, disinhibition of glutamatergic projection neurons has emerged as a prominent circuit motif within the PAG for releasing a variety of behaviors, including freezing (Tovote et al., 2016), pup grooming (Kohl et al., 2018), and antinociception (Morgan and Clayton, 2005)
evidence: Citation to findings from prior studies on PAG circuit organization

claim: PAG-USV neuronal activity is tightly regulated by descending inputs as well as inputs from local GABAergic PAG neurons.
source: Our results support a model in which PAG-USV neuronal activity is tightly regulated by descending inputs as well as inputs from local GABAergic PAG neurons, which in turn integrate a variety of behaviorally relevant forebrain inputs to appropriately gate PAG-USV activity and hence USV production
evidence: Summary of circuit model based on experimental findings

claim: Disinhibitory circuit motifs in the PAG may provide a failsafe mechanism that carefully regulates the behavioral contexts in which crucial but potentially costly behaviors, including vocalization, are produced.
source: More generally, such disinhibitory circuit motifs in the PAG may provide a failsafe mechanism that carefully regulates the behavioral contexts in which crucial but potentially costly behaviors, including vocalization, are produced
evidence: Interpretation of functional significance of circuit organization

source: We note that vocal behavior is not simply binary: in addition to deciding whether or not to vocalize, an animal must produce vocalizations that are appropriate for a given situation
evidence: Statement of conceptual framework about vocal behavior

claim: The elucidation of circuit and synaptic mechanisms through which forebrain inputs to the PAG vocal gating circuit influence USV production represents an important first step toward understanding how forebrain-to-midbrain circuits regulate the production of vocalizations across different behavioral contexts.
source: The elucidation of circuit and synaptic mechanisms through which forebrain inputs to the PAG vocal gating circuit influence USV production represents an important first step toward understanding how forebrain-to-midbrain circuits regulate the production of vocalizations across different behavioral contexts to enable effective communication
evidence: Statement of significance and broader implications of the findings
